sections.text: Governing sense, mind and intellect, intent on liberation, free from desire, fear and anger, the sage is forever free.
Knowing me as Him who gladly receives all offerings of austerity and sacrifice, as the Mighty Ruler of all the Worlds and the Friend of all beings, he passes to Eternal Peace.

We had been discussing chapter 5, Karma Sannyasa Yoga, Yoga of True Renunciation of Actions. We are coming to the concluding part of chapter five -- the last three verses. We have seen previously that Bhagavan said the one who develops qualities appropriate to merge with Brahman, he merges with Brahman.
Yah Antaha Sukhaha Antahramah Tatha Antah Jyotihi Evayaha, Sahayogi Brahmanirvanam, Brahma Bhutodi Gachade. These are the qualifications one must develop if he wants to attain that eternal liberation, to merge with the supreme Self. If he wants to achieve the final goal of complete liberation, he needs to understand that this finite being is not capable of attaining that.
He has to leave attachment to this finite being -- this body, mind, and intellect -- which is running outside seeking happiness. That idea, that happiness lies outside in the world, has to be renounced. And he has to develop qualities where he becomes satisfied within his own self.
Yaha Antaha Sukhaha -- who finds his happiness within himself. Ya Antahramaha -- who revels in his own self. Antah Jyoti -- He reveals his own existence.
I do not need anyone to convince me that I exist. Verification is required for everything else -- whether Im smart, whether Im powerful, whether I achieved anything, am I an architect or not. I need verification for all of that.
But whether I exist? I need no verification. I know the self -- it is self-emerging knowledge. One who relies on that, one who identifies with that -- Sahayogi Brahmanirvanam -- he loses his limited self.
He loses his identity in that greater identity. As we have seen in our analogy, when a small company merges with a big company, the small companys name goes away and it becomes one with the larger company. Labhante Brahma Nirvanam, Rishayah Kshina Kalmashaha.
But to achieve that, you have to become Kshina Kalma -- without any impurities of mind. Those who have purified themselves of all sins, they achieve this Brahma Nirvanam. They dissolve themselves into Brahman.
And we have seen that sin is nothing but the agitations in my mind. As long as I want something out of this world, its a desire. And as long as I dont have it, Im incomplete -- that creates agitation.
If I acquire it, I want to preserve it. That creates another agitation. I accomplished all that.
I have this bank balance in my 401k. It seems Im set for my retirement of what happens if the market collapses and I lose everything. So theres always fear of preserving what I have and also an anxiety about what I have not accomplished.
One who is without this agitation in his mind, whose mind is purified, he attains that ultimate truth. He becomes one with that supreme self. Chinna Dvaidha -- he does not see the duality.
Up till now I have lived my life as an island. The world is outside, competing with me, and I have to get my happiness out of it. So Im constantly in battle with this world as an individual.
If that individuality is dissolved, if I expand my identification -- as we have seen before, right now my ego is concentrated in my limited self which I call myself. If I can expand my ego to include others -- my identification. At a small level, we all do that.
We identify with our family, we identify with our friends, our community, our nation. Therefore, when Brazil was not doing well with coronavirus, we were not that upset. But when India is not doing well -- We are all very disturbed.
Because of identification. I have expanded my identification from just me to the country where I was born and raised, and also the country where I live. Chinna Dvaidha -- they have expanded their identification to include everything.
Yatatmanaha -- one who has control over this limited self. Once I identify with the world, then my purpose becomes seeking the welfare of all beings. So these are the qualifications of the person who wants to achieve liberation -- the Mumukshu, who is desirous of Moksha.
One who is happy the way he is does not need anything to do with this. But one who is not happy with the condition he is in and wants that liberation -- for him, these are the qualifications he has to achieve, that he has to strive for. And then the next three verses -- the last three verses -- are actually introductory verses for the next chapter.
In Sanskrit literature it is very common for the author to introduce a subject at the end of a chapter so that you are ready for the next chapter. Its like in Gujarati magazines -- the story gets very interesting and then it ends and says the more interesting part will be in the next edition. Bhagavan is also using a similar technique.
Hes introducing meditation in these last three verses. These verses are more like sutras, very succinct. The entire process of meditation and the goal is described.
It says Sparshan krutva bahir bahyan, chakshushcha iva antare bhruvoh, prana-apanau samau krutva nasa-abhyantara charinau. Here, the entire technique of meditation is given. The first instruction is Sparshan krutva bahir bahyan -- keep all the sense objects outside, outside of your perception.
So dont let the senses bring the information from outside of the sense objects which then creates these impressions on your mind. You shut off that mechanism of bringing all those impressions from the outside. This is something like if you have an old style camera which has a Kodak film in it.
If you open the shutter, whatever is inside the image will come inside to the lens. And then the film is like your mind. So the film will capture the impression on it.
So there are two ways you can avoid taking any picture. One is you dont open the lens at all. I have done it before -- forgot to remove the cap.
I kept clicking but nothing appeared on the film because the lens was covered. Kathopanishad says you should fold your senses into the mind. The senses are turned inward; they are not looking outwards.
Then there is no experience from outside. Or keep the experience outside only -- dont let it influence your mind. And focus your gaze at the juncture of your eyebrows.
Now that you have turned your gaze inside, you have to focus on your mind. So now the mind is focused, laserized. There are good explanations about the scientific and medical implications of focusing between the eyes.
But from a yogic perspective, we are focused on the Ajna chakra. In our bodies we have six chakras. In some traditions there is a seventh chakra, the Sahasrara chakra, also called Brahmarandra.
Thats your exit point when you die, if you are a Yogi. Bhagavan says here, focus on your Ajna chakra. The Ajna chakra is also called the third eye.
In our literature, Shiva had a third eye -- the eye of wisdom. This third eye or Ajna chakra is associated with the subtle body, the mind and intellect. So rather than focusing on the world outside, now you focus on the world inside -- on your mind and intellect -- and turn them towards this chakra, which is a connection between you and the supreme.
Bhagavan said, Chakshushcha eva antare bruvaha. Focus your attention between the two eyebrows, at the Ajna chakra. It also corresponds to the pineal gland in your physiology.
That is why we have a bindi in our culture at that point, and why the Yogis put Chandan tilak to keep that Ajna chakra protected. Prana Apanau Samau Krutva -- equalizing the prana and apana. We also learnt in chapter three, I think it was verse 29, which says they offer the Prana into Apana or Apana into Prana.
One of the Yajnas is this Prana-Apana Yajna, which is basically Pranayama with retention and breath control. The Rishis developed this great technique after noticing that the mind affects breathing. So if I use that knowledge -- that there is a connection between my mind and my breathing -- I can control breathing to control my mind.
This whole elaborate science of Pranayama was developed based on this principle. So here it says, make Prana and Apana equal. When there is no imbalance between the two, the mind also becomes balanced and controlled.
I have read Dnyaneshwar Maharajs Dnyaneshwari, and it explains this beautifully: combine the power of Prana and Apana together and direct it towards your Sahasrara Chakra. The energy which is right now used for maintaining this body gets equalized so that the body is maintained with very minimal energy, and the rest is focused towards your Sahasrara chakra. According to yogic tradition, we have a connection with our greater self through that chakra.
So Bhagavan says, balance your Prana and Apana -- Nasabhyantara Charinau -- which flow through your nostrils. Yat Indriyaha Manaha Buddhi Munihi Moksha Parayanaha. If you are desirous of liberation, if the goal is to achieve liberation, then you have to make this preparation throughout your life.
It is not something where you get up one morning and start meditating. Bhagavan Buddha did not get up that morning under a Bodhi tree and say, I need to meditate and achieve enlightenment. He had to work all his life to achieve that enlightenment. This is the practice that controls my organs, my senses, my Manas (mind), and my Buddhi (intellect).
This cannot happen overnight, as we know. It is also not going to happen just because you decided to do so. Its a constant practice without any gap.
Eknathi Swaran used to say that if you miss a day in meditation, it takes a week to make up. If you miss a week of meditation, it takes a month to make it up. If you miss a month, it takes a year to make it up.
So its a constant practice to control your organs, control your mind, control intellect. Now we are all doing it. So its not something which is not in our control.
We control over organs in a sense. We dont behave in an inappropriate manner in the public. We also control our mind.
Sometimes we feel like doing something, but we realize its not the right thing to do. So we control our mind. We control intellect too.
Sometimes we get fancy ideas, but then we think, no, thats not the right thing. We do have capabilities. Except our goal is different in using that capability.
Were trying to achieve something from this world. Here it says Moksha Parayanaha -- those who are Mumukshu, those who are desirous of liberation, they use this capability to control mind, intellect, and body in achieving that liberation. Vigata Icchha Bhaya Krodhaha -- this is only possible if youre without desire, fear, and anger.
We know that our life is basically nothing but a permutation and combination of these three. Either we are desirous of getting something, or we are fearful that we may not get it, or we are angry. Thats because my mind is right now turned outside, seeking happiness.
If I realize that happiness does not lie outside -- the world of objects has no capability to give me happiness. As we have seen, every object which gives me happiness has equal capability to give me unhappiness. If thats true, they actually cancel each other out.
It is like particles which have a negative and positive charge -- they cancel each other out and disappear. These objects are illusory. They do not have the essential thing which I am seeking -- happiness.

The final two verses of Chapter 5 bring the teaching to its culmination. Verse 28 describes the sage who is governing sense, mind and intellect and is free from desire, fear and anger - such a one is forever free. Verse 29 then reveals the key to eternal peace: knowing the Divine as the receiver of all sacrifices and austerities, as the Mighty Ruler of all the Worlds, and most beautifully, as the Friend of all beings (suhridam sarva-bhutanam). This friendship of the Divine is not a sentimental notion but a recognition that the deepest reality is not indifferent to us but intimately connected.
Today, contemplate the three aspects of the Divine in verse 29. First, bhoktaram yajna-tapasam - the Divine receives all our efforts, sacrifices, and disciplines. Nothing is wasted; every sincere effort is received. Can you offer your days work with this understanding? Second, sarva-loka-maheshvaram - the Divine is the sovereign of all worlds. This removes the burden of trying to control outcomes. Third, and most transformative, suhridam sarva-bhutanam - the Divine is the friend of all beings, including you. Meditate on this: the ultimate Reality is not a cold, impersonal force but a presence that wishes you well. How would you live differently if you truly felt befriended by existence itself? The chapter concludes with the promise: knowing this, one passes to Eternal Peace. Today, let this friendship be your foundation - approach each moment knowing you are supported by the deepest reality, that the universe is not hostile but hospitable to your awakening.
